tweets.text:
Sean Goedecke 在个人博客发文说，在大型软件项目里，程序员只理解自己负责的那一部分代码是正常的，而且这已经是能做到的最好状态。

确实如此，我基于原文稍微解读和引申一下。

很多人说 AI 写不好程序，因为 AI 不能完整理解代码库，但实际上在大的软件项目中，程序员只理解自己负责的一小部分代码是常态。

想象一下，新人去接手一个历史复杂项目，那么他们短时间只可能理解一部分代码，但这并不妨碍他们去维护项目。

那么以前怎么保证不理解完整代码不会改出问题呢？还得要靠自动化测试来兜底。

一个好的项目，需要配合好充分的自动化测试覆盖，这样就算新手去修改代码，也不至于把正常运行的系统搞崩溃，毕竟改出问题了自动化测试是无法通过的。

并且为了防止新人乱改，还会有 Code Review 配合，这本身也是很好的知识传承手段。

现在让 Agent 干活也是如此，让 Agent 在一个会话上下文中理解整个项目是不现实的，它永远只能部分理解项目，但这并不妨碍 Agent 去修改运行程序。

要保证 Agent 干活的质量，同样也要通过验证手段兜底，自动化测试是必须的，但也无法过度依赖，因为有些测试可能本身就是有问题的；

Code Review 现在也很难保证了，毕竟代码量太大了，人根本看不过来，只能是让 AI Review 大部分代码，人只 Review 最重要的部分。

另外一个有效手段就是让 Agent 自己提供证据，比如我最近最常用的手段就是让 Agent 截图，在开发新功能的时候让它提供新功能截图，修改 bug 的时候提供改之前和改之后的截图对比。

让 Agent 截图，最近还挖掘出来一个用法：就是让 Agent 自己去模拟 API 响应数据，动态生成各种不同场景的截图，都不需要服务端配合，虽然我还没搞明白它是怎么去模拟的。

retweet.text:
没错，就是这样。将人排除在外的、完全的自动化，既不可行也不重要。

重要的是进入循环工程里协作，Agent 在里面，人也投入在里面作为上下文输入，去驱动、引导、验收和反馈……

不要把人和系统看作割裂的，人就是系统的一部分。人也不真正想要完全的自动化，人想要的是自己不擅长、不喜欢的部分的自动化，保留自己喜欢和擅长部分；这些都要在循环工程里通过不断互动去调节出来。

一旦拥抱循环，而非拥抱自动化，我们变得更轻松和富有产出，更不焦虑于系统产出与我无关，我必被淘汰。

我们就是系统的一部分，并有不小的贡献。我们的动机输入、验收反馈、居间引导，虽然不是主要的工作量，但都是关键的动作。

人机协作是人和机器形成一个低内耗的循环系统的协同演进过程。

quoted.text:
Software engineering and research have changed significantly for me.

A big mistake I made early on was trying to automate everything.

Instead of trying to automate everything at once with a bunch of silly and subjective skills, I now spend most of my time helping my coding and research agents write better code and explore novel research ideas.

That's right! I am more involved.

I think this approach works best today, given the current state of coding agents. Not only for coding but for researching as well.

This process has resulted in good patterns codified as loops.

Loops involve automations, but they also include clear, intentional steps you can keep refining to remove jaggedness.

I continually strengthen my loops through verifiers, deterministic steps, context formatting and awareness, memory systems, and evals that steer quality and robustness.

So I agree with other great engineering leaders that our job has fundamentally changed. It's not about using LLMs to help us write code. It's helping the LLM write code better and faster. That's where those loops come into play.

This has significantly reduced error rates and allowed me to expand and scale with coding agents in unbelievable ways. Something I naively expected from my initial, silly, outdated automations.

It feels contradictory at first, since we treat coding agents as solve-it-all intelligence, but it's a system like other traditional systems that requires careful attention to unlock its benefits.

Like my other peers, I believe we are in the early innings. There are more core primitives, interfaces, and experiences to build. For example, we still haven't fully figured out agent swarms.

Coding agents only really started to take off around this time last year. It's unbelievable how much has changed since then.

To be better prepared for what's coming next year, I continue to advocate for gaining deeper knowledge and developing mastery and expertise in your domain. That will continue to matter.

The Lean FRO and Mathlib Initiative have released a joint statement on the Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis.

On November 20, Levent Alpöge released a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as a Lean library of 17 million lines of code. Over the past day, the Lean and Mathlib communities worked together to verify it. The statement certifies the proof as correct and describes how it meets all necessary verification criteria.

Congratulations to Levent on this achievement, and thank you to everyone in the community who contributed to the verification.
